page.title: tinyactors: like SQLite, but for actors
page.description: tinyactors runs millions of statecharts inside your program, in Node.js, Python, a browser or C: composable state machines that describe a reactive system formally.

hero.headline: Like SQLite, but for actors
hero.lede: tinyactors runs millions of actors inside your Node.js, Python, browser or C process, with no separate server. Each actor runs a composable statechart of states, events and transitions.

section.heading: The chart decides, your code acts
section.p: The order actor keeps its cart in its data model, and its chart decides what each event means. When the payment service cannot be reached, the order tries again on its own.

The chart reaches the world only by sending events to an I/O processor, an object your program gives the host. This program's payment service fails the first charge, and the order retries a second later:

section.heading: Deterministic behaviors
section.p: A statechart is a composable state machine of states, events and transitions. Because it isolates effects as events, your code can simulate runs in tests.
A tinyactors actor runs a chart instead of arbitrary code, so your code can simulate and test its events.
tinyactors runs the same chart in simulation and inside your Node.js, Python, browser or C process. Your code steps timeouts on a simulated clock to test each change in milliseconds.

section.heading: Local reasoning for agents
section.p: tinyactors puts all of an actor's states and transitions in one readable, inspectable chart. Your code connects through events, so an agent writes an actor from events entering and leaving, not the full system.
Every effect leaves the chart as an event your code performs, so a review of an agent's change reads one file. Your code can read any running actor's state and data.

section.heading: Run millions of actors in your process

item.text: tinyactors is a library running your program, so you stay in control, and can use actors to model server and client logic.
tinyactors wraps one C core in every language package, and every package runs the W3C SCXML tests.

item.term: Small enough for every part of a system
item.text: Actor instances cost around half a kilobyte of RAM, making them small enough for you to model in-flight API request, WebSocket connection, and domain objects as an actor in tests and production.

section.p: Tinyactors implements virtual actors, allowing you to store idle actors in a store of your choice. Storing actor state in the database you are already using gives you durability across process restarts.
When to use tinyactors compares it with Temporal, Durable Objects, Rivet and XState, and lists its limits.

section.heading: Kill your unit tests
section.p: A unit test checks one run you wrote down. A property is a rule, like "never charge a card more than three times", checked on runs a program generates.

With attempts < 4 in the chart, the loop stops at seed 10: it charged the card four times.

section.heading: Conquer complexity
section.p: A team chat's hard state is who is in each room and who is online. The five-step tutorial puts each part of that state in an actor:

item.text: Two joins at the same moment can overwrite each other in a shared member list. A room actor handles one event at a time, so its member list keeps every join.
A user who stops being active sends no event, so nothing marks them as away. The user's chart restarts a timer on each activity and marks the user away after 300 seconds.

Most users are idle, and each one's data takes memory as long as it stays loaded. An idle user's actor is saved to a store and loaded again on its next event: a thousand users ran with fifty in memory.

section.heading: Run actors in production
section.p: An actor in production stands for an entity, such as an account, and lives as long as it does. So you change and watch actors that are already running.

item.text: When your rules change, the accounts already running still follow the old ones. Add the chart's new version, and a migration moves each running actor to it, keeping the state it reached.
A snapshot copies every actor of a running process, and Host.restore runs it in this process or another. Two million actors, 1000 of them in memory, make a 165 MB snapshot.
tinyactors traces every step of every actor as OpenTelemetry. You turn it on with an option, not with code.
